newsitem.title: USA: USAir says still faces high unit costs.
newsitem.headline: USAir says still faces high unit costs.

text.p: USAir Group Inc's unit costs remain the highest in the airline industry and "seriously restrict" the company's ability to compete with low-cost carriers, USAir chairman and chief executive, Stephen Wolf, said.
Wolf made his remarks in a prepared statement that accompanied the company's fourth quarter and year-end results.
The company earned $0.08 per share, fully diluted, in the quarter, compared with $0.54 per share in the year-earlier period, it said.
USAir's cost per available seat mile rose to $12.77 per share in the period, from $11.87 a year before.
Wolf said USAir suffered from agressive expansion by Delta Air Lines Inc and Southwest Airlines Co in 1996, which combined added 223,000 seats per week in USAir's markets.

The company also said that in 1997 it will make a special payment of $50 million toward preferred dividend arrears to senior preferred stockholders. The company is not currently paying regular preferred stock dividends, it said.
Later in the day a USAir spokesman said that the company still needed to reign in labor and other costs to reduce its unit costs.
"We are in very broad-ranging discussions now with our labor groups," said Rick Weintraub, a USAir spokesman.
Weintraub also said the company's November agreement with Airbus Industrie to acquire 400 aircraft depended on USAir achieving a "competitive cost structure."
He would not say what USAir deemed a "competitive cost structure."
Costs per available seat mile at Delta and Southwest for short flights are about $0.07 per seat mile, compared with around $0.12 per seat mile at USAir, he added.
